RECORD CITATION GLOSSARY
The state-court record involving the prosecution of
crimes against amicus B.R. is available in the Utah Court
of Appeals. Utah v. Trevino , Case No. 20240654-CA.
The appeal is from guilty verdicts in Utah v. Trevino ,
201907429 (3d Dis. Utah 2025). Amicus B.R. cites the
testimony and other information in the record by the short
form “R” for court of appeals record.

1
INTEREST OF AMICUS CURIAE1
Amicus B.R. is the victim of multiple child sexual
abuse crimes committed against her in Utah. 2 An eightperson jury considered and rendered guilty verdicts on
those charges. Those verdicts are currently on direct
appeal to the Utah Court of Appeals. B.R. has an interest
in this Court upholding the constitutionality of convictions
rendered by eight-person juries, including the convictions
in her case.
STATEMENT
For 130 years, Utah has relied on eight-person juries
to decide non-capital criminal cases. More than fifty
years ago, this Court squarely held that Utah’s approach
complied with the Constitution. See Williams v. Florida ,
399 U.S. 78 (1970).
In deciding whether to overturn precedent, this
Court has looked to “reliance on the decision” in question
as an important factor to weigh in the balance. See, e.g.,
Ramos v. Louisiana , 590 U.S. 83, 106 (2020). Here, the
Court should give heavy weight to the reliance interests of
crime victims like B.R., who have come forward to testify
before eight-person juries. Overturning Williams would
1.  Pursuant to Sup. Ct. R. 37.6, amicus affirms that this
brief was not authored in whole or in part by any party or counsel
for any party and that no person or entity other than amicus or
her counsel made a monetary contribution to its preparation or
submission.
2.  As a juvenile victim of a sexual assault crime, B.R.
proceeds pseudonymously here through her initials.

2
potentially imperil duly obtained convictions rendered
by juries with fewer than twelve members in Utah and
elsewhere—including the convictions rendered in B.R.’s
case. The Court should decline the invitation to unsettle
such long-settled law.
FACTUAL BACKGROUND REGARDING B.R.
The conviction in B.R.’s case—currently on appeal
to the Utah Court of Appeals—serves to illustrate how
she and thousands of other crime victims in Utah and
elsewhere have relied on this Court’s previous decisions
allowing states to use juries with fewer than twelve
persons.
Twenty-nine-year-old Rudolfo Trevino found thirteenyear-old B.R. via Facebook in late 2017. After previous
failed attempts at getting B.R. alone in his vehicle, in
February 2018, he raped her. R1002. At his request, she
had met him in his truck. Id. They talked briefly and he
tried to kiss her. Id. When she refused, he placed himself
on top of her, removed her pants, and forced his penis into
her vagina. Id.
Ignoring B.R.’s physical resistance and her screams
of “no,” “it hurts,” and “stop,” Trevino told her to “shut
the fuck up, to just moan.” R1002-03. He withdrew in time
to ejaculate on her stomach. R1003. She was revolted and
confused, not knowing what semen was. Id. Laughing at
her naïveté, Trevino threw a roll of paper towels at her
and told her to clean it up. Id. Afterward, Trevino sent
her a text message making what happened clear, “Well,
yeah, I just took your virginity.” R1641 .

3
After the first rape, B.R. was “confused” and “lost and
stopped caring” about life. R1008. She attempted suicide.
But throughout 2018 and into 2019, Trevino regularly
pressured her into oral sex, intercourse, and other sexual
acts in his house and car. R1009, 1086, 1098-99.
If B.R. refused to come over or participate, Trevino
“would get really mad,” “say he would hurt me,” or
“threaten my family.” He would hit her, hold guns to his
own head or point guns at B.R. R1007-08.
Trevino controlled B.R. when they were not together,
physically restricting her access to her phone, visiting
her junior high school, and demanding she send him inclass photos of herself to prove her whereabouts. He took
pictures and videos of him and B.R. during intercourse
and other sexual acts. If she hesitated, he would threaten
to send B.R.’s previous nudes to other people. “[S]cared
to be in trouble with cops,” B.R. kept their interactions
hidden. R1009, 1012.
By May 2019, B.R. was attending her junior high
school dance, when she received messages from Trevino,
demanding she leave the dance with him because he
thought she was “with another guy.” After Trevino picked
up B.R., officers stopped the vehicle. Trevino ordered B.R.
to run, which resulted in B.R. being tased while Trevino
assaulted the officers and was arrested. R1012-13.
From jail, Trevino sent messages to B.R., threatening
suicide if she did not get his charges dismissed. When
B.R. met with a forensic interviewer a few months later,
her interview was “short, and [she] was very reluctant…
to say anything to anybody.”

4
In April 2020, the trial court entered a permanent
criminal stalking injunction, ordering Trevino to stay
1,000 feet away from B.R.’s home and work and to not
“threaten,” “harass,” “communicate, contact or follow”
B.R. R70.
But just weeks later, on May 18, Trevino again began
sending B.R. threatening text messages. A day later,
Trevino broke into B.R.’s bedroom where she was asleep
and demanded that she “go with him” or he would “hurt
her.” R1026-27, 1032, 1120-22.
On June 22, as B.R. stood waiting at a bus stop,
Trevino and an accomplice swerved to a stop in their
van, threw the sliding door open, and chased B.R. on foot.
R1078-80, 1124, 1291. With the help of passersby, B.R.
escaped into a nearby business. R1079, 1285, 1292.
The years of abuse had finally pushed B.R. past her
breaking point. Now 15, B.R. realized she was just “a kid,”
and asked herself, “How am I going to get in trouble?”
Feeling “overwhelmed,” she told her mother she “needed
to talk to [the police] because things are getting out of
control.”
After a missing person report raised police suspicions,
Trevino was ordered to the probation office. R1358. On
Trevino’s phone was a video of Trevino and B.R. having sex.
When asked to identify his sex partner, Trevino claimed
not to know who it was. In a search incident to arrest for
violation of probation, staff confiscated a microSD card
from Trevino’s wallet. The SD card contained over 600
images of B.R., including 39 nude images. R1329, 1345-46.

5
Although B.R. thought Trevino was in jail, she still
feared for her safety and traded rooms with her mother.
Thus, it was her mother sleeping in that bedroom the night
of June 26 when she awoke to the sound of the window
screen being removed. Her mother saw Trevino, dressed
all in black, looking in through the window. R1397-1404,
1451-52.
On June 28, B.R. met with the police to report the
abuse. Trevino was then arrested—an arrest that took a
SWAT team, chemical munitions, and a K9 unit to drag
Trevino out. R1397–1404.
Trevino was charged with rape of a child, stalking,
attempted burglary, two counts of rape, two counts of
forcible sexual abuse, and ten counts of sexual exploitation
of a minor.
Following Utah’s 130-year-old procedure (enshrined
in the State’s Constitution), the judge empaneled an
eight-member jury. Trevino did not argue that number
was unfair or unconstitutional. At Trevino’s three-day
jury trial, the State presented evidence of the events
outlined above through the testimony of more than fifteen
witnesses and more than two hundred exhibits.
For the prosecution to pursue the case, B.R. had to
give detailed and graphic testimony about many of the
images found on Trevino’s phone, including in-depth
explanations of each of the ten images depicting her being
abused while a minor by Trevino. She was also forced to
describe specific sexual acts Trevino subjected her to in
the images, which constituted child sex abuse materials
(CSAM). R1089–97.

6
Ultimately, the jury found Trevino guilty on sixteen
out of seventeen charges. The trial court sentenced
Trevino to an aggregate term of 37 years to life and
recommended that the parole board not consider parole,
noting that while it “rarely” had “occasion to say this …
incapacitation is the object.” R452-56, 1665–69.
Trevino timely appealed, and his appeal is pending
before the Utah Court of Appeals. In a victim impact
statement submitted to that court, B.R. explained that
merely learning of the appeal “sent me into a panic
attack.” She described severe anxiety, nightmares, and
post-traumatic stress disorder, and explained that because
she had testified against Trevino, she lives in fear that he
“would want to retaliate against me.” His incarceration,
she wrote, “gives me a sense of security that I can try
to live my life.” Victim Impact Statement of B.R., Utah
v. Trevino, 20240654-CA (Utah Ct. App. May 11, 2026).
SUMMARY OF THE ARGUMENT
This Court should not overturn Williams . Crime
victims have relied on the constitutionality of their state
jury trial procedures in making decisions about entering
the criminal justice system. This Court should give these
strong and reasonable reliance interests heavy weight in
its stare decisis analysis and decline to overrule Williams.
Moreover, neither Petitioner nor his amici  can
point to specific problems stemming from using fewerthan-twelve-person juries. For example, the available
data indicate that there is no higher risk of convicting
factually innocent defendants when using smaller juries
compared to using twelve-person juries. The absence

7
of empirically proven real-world harms strongly favors
retaining Williams.
Finally, if this Court nonetheless decides to overturn
Williams , it should recognize that a criminal trial by
fewer than twelve jurors can be harmless error in cases
(such as B.R.’s) where the evidence of a defendant’s guilt
is overwhelming. Where no reasonable juror could have
a different assessment of the evidence, a retrial would
be a pointless exercise—and one that would be very
traumatizing to crime victims.
ARGUMENT
I. The Court Should Not Overrule Williams Because
Crime Victims Have Strong Reliance Interests at
Stake.
This Court has explained that stare decisis is the
“foundation . . . of the rule of law.” Kisor v. Wilkie , 588
U.S. 558, 586 (2019) (quoting Michigan v. Bay Mills
Indian Cmty., 572 U.S. 782, 798 (2014)). Therefore, this
Court should apply stare decisis principles dependably
from case-to-case. Consistent application of stare decisis
“permits society to presume that bedrock principles
are founded in the law rather than in the proclivities of
individuals, and thereby contributes to the integrity of our
constitutional system of government, both in appearance
and in fact.” Vasquez v. Hillery , 474 U.S. 254, 265–66
(1986); accord Ramos v. Louisiana , 590 U.S. 83, 121
(2020) (Kavanaugh, J., concurring) (noting the need “to
apply stare decisis  principles in a neutral and consistent
manner”).

8
This Court typically does not overrule its precedents—
even a decision interpreting the Constitution—without a
“special justification.” Ramos, 590 U.S. at 120 (Kavanaugh,
J., concurring) (quoting Allen v. Cooper, 589 U.S. 248, 259
(2020)). In determining whether a sufficient justification
exists, the Court has traditionally examined whether
the prior decision was “egregiously wrong,” whether
overruling it would “unduly upset reliance interests,” and
whether the prior decision “has caused significant negative
jurisprudential or real-world consequences.” Id. at 121–22.
Williams v. Florida, 399 U.S. 78 (1970), was correctly
decided, as Florida and its supporting amici (including
Utah) have persuasively explained. But even if one were
to assume Williams was somehow egregiously wrong,
the remaining stare decisis factors  strongly support
upholding the decision. Specifically, among other reasons,
crime victims have relied upon Williams and no empirical
evidence suggests that Williams has caused an increase
in wrongful convictions.
A. Crime Victims Have Reasonably Relied on the
Constitutionality of Their States’ Jury-Trial
Systems.
Just as stare decisis is the foundation for the
rule of law, see Kisor , 588 U.S. at 586, reliance is the
cornerstone in that foundation. The justification for stare
decisis is ultimately premised on the need for stability
and predictability— i.e., the ability of individuals and
institutions to rely upon this Court’s precedents. See,
e.g., Payne v. Tennessee , 501 U.S. 808, 827 (1991); see
also Amy Coney Barrett, Precedent and Jurisprudential
Disagreement , 91 Tex. L. Rev. 1711,  1730 (2013) (“while

9
[stare decisis] serves many goals, the protection of reliance
interests is paramount.” (footnote omitted)). Therefore,
“[i]n some cases, reliance provides a strong reason for
adhering to established law.” Janus v. State, County, &
Mun. Emps., 585 U.S. 878, 926 (2018).
Victims like B.R. have an interest in the stability of
the criminal-justice system, and specifically in avoiding
retrials based on shifting constitutional rules. B.R.’s case
well illustrates this interest.
B.R. was sexually abused for years before she finally
made the difficult decision to report Trevino’s sexual
assaults. And once Trevino had been arrested, B.R. made
the still more difficult decision to testify at his trial. In
doing so, she recounted the lengthy history of his sexual
abuse and Trevino’s efforts at manipulation. She even was
required to review her own child sexual abuse materials
(CSAM), identifying her nipples and vagina. And she was
cross-examined at length.
Empirical research supports that victims—and
specifically victims of violent crimes—suffer severe
trauma not just from the criminal act itself, but also from
recounting the act before others in pursuit of justice. E.g.,
Uli Orth, Secondary Victimization of Crime Victims
by Criminal Proceedings , 15 Social J. Rsch. 313, 316,
321 (2002) (compiling studies); Rebecca Campbell, The
Psychological Impact of Rape Victims’ Experiences
with the Legal, Medical, and Mental Health Systems ,
63 Am. Psych. 702, 703–05 (2008) (same). Indeed, some
victims—particularly victims of sexual assault—choose
not to report crimes in part because they do not wish to
endure the traumas associated with the criminal justice

10
system. E.g., Rachael Goodman-Williams et al., Reasons
for Not Reporting Among Sexual Assault Survivors Who
Seek Medical Forensic Exams: A Qualitative Analysis ,
39 J. Interpersonal Violence 1905, 1907, 1913–14 (2024);
Negar Katirai, Retraumatized in Court , 62 Ariz. L. Rev.
82, 96-98 (2025). Victims like B.R. understand that they
will be asked to recount their traumatic experiences
but nonetheless do so to achieve justice and closure. But
victims do not come forward to go through an essentially
meaningless exercise—an exercise that Petitioner claims
leads to “no verdict at all.” Pet. Br. at 19 (citation omitted).
This Court has cautioned that “in the administration
of criminal justice, courts may not ignore the concerns of
victims.” Morris v. Slappy, 461 U.S. 1, 14 (1983). Of course,
in the normal course of a criminal case, “inconvenience
and embarrassment to witnesses cannot justify failing to
enforce constitutional rights of an accused.” Id. But the
different question presented here is whether the Court
should overrule longstanding precedent and chart a new
course that directly harms victims.
In making its decision, this Court should consider
the interests of victims such as B.R. in avoiding retrials.
B.R.’s experience in the initial trial was extremely
traumatizing; but Trevino’s conviction has resulted in a
modicum of closure and allowed B.R. to move on. If this
Court overturns Williams, the potential resulting retrial
could require B.R. to go through that ordeal once again—
further prolonging what is already a nightmare lasting
more than eight years. Retrials naturally exacerbate
the harms to victims, particularly because they involve
extreme delay in reaching a final decision and achieving
a modicum of closure for the victim. See Diane M. Daane,

11
Victim Response to Sexual Assault , in sexUal assaUlt:
the VICtIms, the PerPetrators, and the CrImInal jUstICe
system  93, 111 (Frances Reddington & Betsy Wright
Kreisel eds., 3d ed. 2017) (“It is common for a rape victim
to have setbacks when she experiences another trauma, and
especially when she again becomes involved in the criminal
justice proceeding of her rape case.”). Cf. Vestina Virsilaite,
The Impact of Court Delays on Sexual Assault and Rape
Survivors’ Psychological Well-Being and Perceptions of
Justice, J. Crime & Just. Dissertations 10–12, 18 (2025)
(“[D]espite the judicial system’s aim to provide justice,
prolonged delays and adversarial procedures contribute
to further suffering, deterring survivors from seeking or
continuing legal action altogether”).
To be sure, when B.R. made the decisions to report
her abuse and later to testify about it, she did not have
full understanding of all the details of this Court’s Sixth
Amendment jurisprudence. But she could reasonably
expect that the system she chose to enter was one that
courts had reviewed and validated. For 130 years, Utah
has used eight-person juries in non-capital felony cases.
See Utah Const., Art. I. § 10 (1896). In Utah, it is simply
untrue that when “ordinary citizens picture a jury deciding
someone’s fate, they picture twelve.” Br. of 38 Current and
Former Prosecutors at 16. Indeed, the constitutionality of
this eight-juror system, as applied to crimes committed
after statehood, has never been questioned by this Court
or the Utah Supreme Court. 3 And for the last 56 years,
3.  In Thompson v. Utah , this Court held that Utah violated
the Ex Post Facto  Clause by using an eight-person jury to try a
defendant for an act committed while Utah was a territory subject
to territorial laws, which specifically required twelve-person
juries. See 170 U.S. 343, 345, 355 (1898), overruled by  Collins v.

12
Utah has operated its jury system under the explicit
blessing of this Court. See Williams, 399 U.S. at 86; see
also Johnson v. Turner , 429 F .2d 1152, 1154 (10th Cir.
1970) (holding that Williams dictates that Utah’s eightperson jury system is constitutional).
Against this backdrop, B.R. relied on the constitutionality
of eight-person juries. To put things plainly, if B.R. had
been told at the outset that her painful and traumatizing
trip through the criminal justice system would end up
producing “no verdict at all,” she would never have gone
through it.4 And if Williams is overruled, she—and many
others like her—may yet decide not to testify at a retrial.
Youngblood, 497 U.S. 37, 47, 51–52 (1990); see also 2 Comp. Laws of
Utah § 3065 (1888), repealed by, Utah Const. Art. I, § 10 (1896) (“A
trial jury in a district court consists of twelve.”). While the Court
explained in dicta its interpretation of the Sixth Amendment,
see Thompson , 170 U.S. at 349,  that decision is best understood
as expressing no opinion on the constitutionality of states using
fewer-than-twelve-person juries. Indeed, Utah courts uniformly
understood Thompson  this way. See, e.g., State v. Hart, 57 P. 415,
416 (Utah 1899); State v. Rock, 57 P. 532, 532 (Utah 1899); State v.
Bates, 61 P. 905, 906 (Utah 1900). The use of eight-person juries
to try non-capital felonies has continued in Utah undisturbed for
the 128 years since Thompson .
4.  One of Petitioner’s amici raises concerns that crime victim
reporting will decline if the existing regime is left in place. Br. of
38 Current and Former Prosecutors at 3–4. No evidence supports
that claim and, to the contrary, overturning numerous otherwisevalid sexual assault convictions seems far more likely to reduce
victim reporting, since victims would associate the justice system
with a meaningless, traumatic exercise in futility. Cf. U.S. Dept.
of Justice, Bureau Just. Stat., Criminal Victimization, 2024  tbl.
4 (2025) (reporting of sexual assault victimization fell from 46.0%
in 2023 to 23.6% in 2024).

13
See Morris, 461 U.S. at 14 (cautioning that unwarranted
reversals “would hardly encourage victims to report
violations to the proper authorities” particularly “when the
crime is one calling for public testimony about a humiliating
and degrading experience”). This Court should weigh
these interests of crime victims in considering whether
to overrule Williams.
B. Crime Victims’ Reliance Interests Are
Significant.
In the stare decisis analysis, reliance interests can
be given varying weight. For example, stare decisis  is
at its “acme in cases involving property and contract
rights, where reliance interests are involved; the opposite
is true in cases . . . involving procedural and evidentiary
rules.” Payne, 501 U.S. at 828 (citations omitted); but see
Ramos, 590 U.S. at 113 (Sotomayor, J., concurring) (“[T]he
force of stare decisis  is at its nadir in cases concerning
criminal procedure rules that implicate fundamental
constitutional protections.” (citation modified) (quoting
Alleyne v. United States, 570 U.S. 99, 116 n.5 (2013))). But
it is not true that all cases involving procedural rules fail
to generate strong reliance interests. Indeed, “the force
of stare decisis  is reduced” only when procedural rules
“do not govern primary conduct and do not implicate the
reliance interests of private parties.” Alleyne, 570 U.S. at
119. As explained above, procedural rules, and particularly
the act of altering procedural rules, implicate the primary
conduct of crime victims—notably victims of sexual
assault—who must make life-changing decisions based
on the likelihood that reporting crimes and testifying at
trial will improve their lives.

14
It would be a mistake to read this Court’s stare decisis
cases as foreclosing any reliance on procedural rules.
Instead, in several earlier cases, the facts simply did not
present legitimate reliance interests.
For example, in Payne, the Court observed that
criminal defendants could not have relied on the rule that
“the Eighth Amendment bars the admission of victim
impact evidence during the penalty phase of a capital
trial.” 501 U.S. at 811, 828. This conclusion is obvious.
It is common sense that the evidence available at trial
and sentencing generally does not factor into capital
defendants’ decision-making. And even if it did, the Court
would not want to encourage murderers’ advance planning
in such a manner.
Similarly, in Alleyne, this Court overruled precedent
and applied Apprendi’s jury-factfinding requirement to
federal mandatory-minimum sentencing enhancements.
See 570 U.S. at 116–18. Crime victims do not have an
interest in a defendant receiving a particular sentence—
they do not enter the criminal justice system in reliance
on a particular punishment outcome. Nor could they, with
the complexities of state and federal sentencing systems
making such outcomes all but impossible to predict in
advance. Moreover, crime victims sometimes disagree
with the prosecutor’s efforts to maximize punishment.
See Paul G. Cassell, On the Importance of Listening to
Crime Victims … Merciful and Otherwise , 102 Tex. L.
Rev. 1381, 1382, 1402–07 (2024). Moreover, the overruling
of precedent in Alleyne resulted in only new sentencing
hearings; it did not require retrials. Therefore, the
mandatory-minimum procedures at issue in Alleyne did
not implicate anyone’s significant reliance interests.

15
By contrast, here crime victims such as B.R. have
relied on the constitutionality and stability of the criminaljustice system when making decisions to report crimes
and testify at trials. Unlike other procedural-error
cases (such as Payne and Alleyne), overruling Williams
would possibly necessitate retrials in thousands of cases
in numerous states, 5 thereby directly implicating the
interests of thousands of crime victims.
To be sure, in Ramos, this Court suggested that
Apodaca v. Oregon, 406 U.S. 404 (1972), engendered only
insignificant reliance interests. See 590 U.S. at 107 (“No
one, it seems, has signed a contract, entered a marriage,
purchased a home, or opened a business based on the
expectation that, should a crime occur, at least the accused
may be sent away on a 10-to-2 verdict.”). But Ramos
involved a procedure (accepting a non-unanimous verdict)
that was implicated in only some cases, and therefore,
did not threaten the stability of the entire  criminal
justice system in Louisiana and Oregon. Moreover, no
one specifically presented the reliance interests of crime
victims to the Court; thus, Ramos seemingly considered
only the reliance interests of the states qua states. See
590 U.S. at 108–09; see also id. at 109–11 (plurality).
A plurality in Ramos  likewise suggested that
Louisiana’s and Oregon’s interests in avoiding retrial of “a
slice of their prior criminal cases” did not outweigh “the
reliance interests of the American people” in preserving
5.  Unless of course the Court acts preemptively to limit the
real-world impact of its decision by, for example, limiting retrials
to those cases where any jury-size error was truly prejudicial. See
infra Part II (urging the Court to do exactly that).

16
“our constitutionally promised liberties.” Id. at 110–11
(plurality). But if this were the end of the analysis, then
in all constitutional cases, the Court could simply consider
only the first stare decisis factor (whether the prior
decision was correctly decided) and then dispense with
the rest. An exclusive focus on the defendant’s assertion
of “constitutionally protected liberties” is plainly not this
Court’s practice—nor should it be.
A final distinction between Apodaca and Williams
is worth emphasizing. Louisiana’s and Oregon’s reliance
on Apodaca always rested “on shaky ground,” given the
fractured holding, id. a t  95  ( p l ur ali ty ) ,  an d  i ts  c o nfli c t
with “two lines” of precedent, id. at 125 (Kavanaugh, J.,
concurring); see also id. at 112 (Sotomayor, J., concurring
(“Apodaca is a universe of one.”)). Here Williams stands
on a much firmer foundation. It would be a seismic shift
for this Court to now tell numerous states—and victims in
these states—that their reliance on the constitutionality
of their long-standing jury systems was misplaced.
In sum, while crime victims in the states implicated
here have not structured their private legal relationships
(i.e., formed a contract, purchased property, or entered a
marriage) based on Williams, they have structured their
public affairs on the basic understanding that a given
state’s criminal-justice system is constitutional. Because
of Williams, crime victims such as B.R. have “legitimate
expectations,” id. at 122 (Kavanaugh, J., concurring), that
the jury verdicts reached in their cases were valid. These
“legitimate expectations” by victims “who have reasonably
relied on . . . precedent,” id., should be weighed heavily in
the stare decisis  balance.

17
C. Williams Has Not Caused Harm, and in
Particular Has Not Increased the Likelihood
of Wrongful Convictions.
A prior decision’s “real-world effects on the citizenry”
are a key factor in determining whether to overturn
the precedent. Ramos, 590 U.S. at 122 (Kavanaugh, J.,
concurring). Florida and its supporting amici have clearly
explained why Williams has not produced any significant
real-world harm. This fact distinguishes this case from
Ramos. By definition, the non-unanimous jury rule was
triggered only in criminal cases where convictions were
most debatable—i.e., where at least one presumably
reasonable juror disagreed with a guilty verdict. Here,
Williams’ holding allowing fewer than twelve jurors
applies to a broad swath of cases where there is no reason
to doubt the outcome—such as B.R.’s case.
Petitioner and a few of his supporting amici, however,
attempt to conjure the specter of innocent defendants
being uniquely at risk when tried by smaller juries.
But whether overturning Williams would specifically
reduce the number of innocent defendants convicted is an
empirical question, requiring consideration of competing
possibilities. For example, Petitioner and his amici
suggest that adding additional jurors could help detect
issues relating to the prosecution’s proof that would have
gone undiscovered by fewer jurors. But on the other
hand, it might be the case that adding several additional
jurors would lead to “free-riding” behavior, where jurors
pay less attention because they think that the multiple
other jurors are doing the work—increasing the risk of
wrongful conviction. See Kaushik Mukhopadhaya, Jury
Size and the Free Rider Problem, 19 J.L. Econ. & Org. 24,

18
40 (2003). Evidence also suggests that larger juries create
“informational cascades,” where a single juror who might
have been ready to vote to acquit on a smaller jury gives
in to more jurors with a contrary view on a larger jury.
See Barbara Luppi & Francesco Parisi, Jury Size and the
Hung-Jury Paradox, 42 J. Legal Stud. 399, 408–09 (2013).
Without carefully weighing the competing concerns,
a few of Petitioner’s amici suggest that this Court should
essentially assume that juries smaller than twelve
jurors produce more wrongful convictions. See, e.g.,
Innocence Project Br. at 7–9. But theoretical speculation
about group dynamics cannot be the correct metric for
whether Williams creates appreciable risks of erroneous
convictions. Cf. Free v. Peters , 12 F .3d 700, 705–06 (7th
Cir. 1994) (en banc) (rejecting mock jury research because
there is little reason to think it can “offer insight into
the ability of a real jury, which has spent days or weeks
becoming familiar with the case ….”). Which way the
balance tips—or if it tips at all—is an empirical question
that must be decided by looking at real-world jury
decisions.
Amicus  Innocence Project cites nine allegedly
“innocent” individuals convicted by juries in the seven
states allowing juries with fewer than twelve individuals.
See Innocence Project Br. at 2 (citing cases from the
National Registry of Exonerations). But there are two
problems with the Innocence Project’s list: First, even
assuming these nine persons are all “innocent,” 6 the
6.  One can debate whether the individuals listed are truly
“innocent,” as the Innocence Project proclaims, Innocence Project
Br. at 2, or are instead individuals whom the prosecution only

19
Innocence Project’s examples are dated. The Project cites
only two cases from the twenty-first century—with the
last one from 2007. This paucity of recent cases may be
because “we should expect the wrongful conviction rate
in this country to have exhibited a decisive downward
trend over the last several decades,” as new and improved
technologies assist law enforcement in prosecuting only
the guilty. See Cassell, supra, at 838–44.
Second, the Innocence Project’s list seems designed
to create the impression that jury size was the cause of
the allegedly wrongful convictions. But for purposes of
this case, the relevant question is not whether “[i]nnocent
people have repeatedly been convicted by non-twelveperson juries.” Innocence Project Br. at 9. Over the last
several decades, the seven states using smaller juries have
undoubtedly prosecuted hundreds of thousands of felony
criminal cases. Even if the risk of an innocent person
being wrongfully convicted is extremely low, see Cassell,
Overstating America’s Wrongful Conviction Rate, supra,
60 Ariz. L. Rev. at 852 (concluding that the risk appears
failed to prove guilt beyond a reasonable doubt. The Project’s
list comes from the National Registry of Exonerations, which
broadly counts as an “exonerated” person many people who
have had their conviction set aside for reasons other than proven
“innocence.” See Paul G. Cassell, Overstating America’s Wrongful
Conviction Rate? Reassessing the Conventional Wisdom About
the Prevalence of Wrongful Convictions , 60 Ariz. L. Rev. 815,
828 n.66 (2018). For example, while one of the Project’s listed
“innocent” persons (Richard Paey) was ultimately pardoned,
the pardon appears principally to have been an act of clemency
responding to an extraordinarily severe sentence—not an
innocence determination. See Paey v. State, 943 So. 2d 919, 920–24
(Fla. Dist. Ct. App. 2006).

20
to be lower than that of being struck by lightning), some
isolated instances of wrongful convictions are essentially
inevitable in a vast sea of criminal prosecutions. Therefore,
the key issue is a comparative one: whether the risk of
wrongful convictions is higher in states using juries with
fewer than twelve jurors than in the other states.
In Ramos, the Innocence Project filed an amicus brief
presenting such comparative data. The Project explained
that Louisiana had the nation’s second-highest Registry
exoneration rate and attributed that high rate to the
State’s non-unanimous-jury rule. See Br. of Innocence
Project et al. as Amici in Support of Petitioner, at 30–31,
Ramos v. Louisiana , 590 U.S. 83 (2020) (No. 18-5924).
But now, a few years later, the Innocence Project never
attempts to compare the Registry exoneration rate in
Florida and six other states using smaller juries for felony
trials with the exoneration rate in those states using
twelve-person juries.
Perhaps the reason that the Innocence Project
fails to make a comparison is that, inconveniently for
its argument, the relevant comparison shows a lower
exoneration rate in the states using fewer than twelve
jurors in felony cases. 7 Using the Innocence Project’s
7.  To permit verification and replication of the data presented
here, an appendix to this brief recounts the exact figures and
sources used. See infra , Appendix.
As Florida points out in its merits brief, while seven states
use smaller-than-twelve-person juries in felony cases, a total of
27 states use such juries for some of their misdemeanor cases. See
Florida Br. at 40–41 n.10. This brief’s calculations focus exclusively
on the seven states using smaller juries for felony cases. Making
an adjustment for misdemeanor cases would not significantly

21
chosen source—the National Registry of Exonerations—
since 1989 8 there have been 3,684 exonerations in state
cases.9 Because this case involves Florida, it is informative
to compare Florida’s per capita exoneration rate 10—with
the national average:

alter the figures presented here, since registry exonerations only
rarely involve misdemeanors. See Nat’l Registry of Exonerations ,
Explore Exonerations, https://exonerationregistry.org/cases
(“Misdemeanor” case characteristic: 122 of 3,863 exonerations
since 1989 or 3.2%).
8.  DNA evidence became available in 1989, which was
the “dawn of a new era” of exonerations. See Information,
“Exoneration Era,” https://exonerationregistry.org/cases . The
National Registry conveniently breaks out this modern era (1989
to date) from earlier data. Id.
9.  As of September 30, 2026, the registry lists 3,863

(e.g., federal court, the District of Columbia, Puerto Rico, and

11.  It would likely be better to calculate an exoneration rate
per violent crime rather than per capita, since jury trials depend on

22
It is also possible to compare the Registry exoneration
rate since 1989 for all seven states that use smaller juries
(assuming, generously, that every exoneration case
involves a sub-twelve-member jury12) with the exoneration
rate in the other 43 states.

Drilling into the data a bit more, one very interesting
point emerges. Of the seven states, the state with the
highest per capita Registry exoneration rate is Louisiana.
The Innocence Project has attributed this high exoneration
rate to Louisiana’s (previously existing) non-unanimous
jury rule. See Ramos v. Louisiana , Br. of Innocence
Project et al. as Amicus in Support of Petitioner, supra,
at 30–31. This attribution suggests that, to avoid the
potential confounding effect of non-unanimous juries on
the existence of a crime rather than the existence of a person. But
to maintain consistency with the Innocence Project’s methodology,
we report per capita figures here. Based on a preliminary review,
switching to per-violent-crime figures would not significantly
change the comparisons discussed in text.
12.  In the seven states, twelve-person juries are used for some
serious cases, such as capital cases.

23

out of the seven states discussed above (and likewise with
Oregon, which also used non-unanimous juries, which
should be backed out of the 43 states). With those two
adjustments, the comparison shows:

Once again, the states with fewer-than-twelve jurors
have a significantly lower exoneration rate.
Pointing in the same direction as these figures, a
detailed empirical study of jurisdiction-specific conviction
rates found a lower error rate in Utah (with eight-person
juries) than North Carolina (with twelve-person juries).
See Paul G. Cassell, Jurisdiction-Specific Wrongful
Conviction Rate Estimates: The North Carolina and
Utah Examples, 60 Ariz. L. Rev. 891, 897–900, 907 (2018)
(estimating an actual-innocence rate for North Carolina
between 0.023% and 0.090%, with a rate for Utah between
0.017% and 0.066%).
In light of these comparisons, it seems likely that the
causes of wrongful conviction lie elsewhere than in the
number of jurors who consider the evidence. Indeed, the

24
National Registry of Exonerations identifies the leading
factors as perjury or false accusation, official misconduct,
mistaken witness identification, misleading forensic
evidence, and the like.13 Jury size is not listed as a factor.
Of course, these calculations do not definitely prove
that states using fewer than twelve jurors have lower
wrongful conviction rates than the other states. Several
caveats should accompany such calculations, including
possible differences between states in how Registry
exonerations are reported. But none of these caveats
were discussed in the Innocence Project’s 2019 amicus
brief in Ramos . Thus, just as the Innocence Project
pointed to Louisiana’s high rate of exonerations under
the non-unanimity rule at issue in that case, it seems
equally fair to highlight the lower rate of exonerations in
Florida’s and the six other states using, in felony cases,
the sub-twelve-person juror rule at issue in this case.
Against that backdrop, there do not appear to be any
proven “significant … real-world consequences” (Ramos,
590 U.S. at 122 (Kavanaugh, J., concurring)) that would
justify overruling Williams.
D. Different Judicial Methodologies Do Not
Render Prior Decisions “Egregiously Wrong.”
Petitioner argues that Williams was wrongly decided
because it conflicts with the original public meaning of
the Sixth Amendment. Pet. Br. at 29–30. Not so. Florida
demonstrates persuasively that Williams was correctly
decided under this Court’s current jurisprudence, which
13.  See Nat’l Registry of Exonerations, Understanding the
Registry, https://exonerationregistry.org/understanding-registry .

25
relies on history for principles rather than exact matches.
See Florida Br. at 22 (citing United States v. Rahimi, 602
U.S. 680, 692 (2024)).
But even assuming that Williams was insufficiently
originalist or erred in its application of that methodology,
that would be no reason to jettison it. Put succinctly, that
a prior decision may have “used different interpretive
tools” than are now in vogue “is not a reason on its own to
discard precedent.” Ramos, 590 U.S. at 112 (Sotomayor, J.,
concurring); see also Loper Bright Enters. v. Raimondo ,
603 U.S. 369, 412 (2024) (“By overruling Chevron, though,
the Court does not call into question prior cases that relied
on the Chevron  framework.”). Were it otherwise, the
Court would need to constantly revisit earlier decisions
that were, arguably, decided with differing approaches.
For example, were this Court to overrule Williams, to
maintain consistency, this Court would presumably also
need to overrule Mapp, Miranda, and a host of other
decisions. See Florida Br. at 5, 45–49.
The exclusionary rule this Court created in Mapp
v. Ohio , 367 U.S. 643 (1961), bears no connection to
the Fourth Amendment’s original public meaning. See
generally Office of Legal Pol’y, U.S. Dept. of Justice,
Report to the Attorney General on the Search and Seizure
Exclusionary Rule  (1986), reprinted in 22 U. Mich. J.L.
Reform 573 (1989). As one scholar has explained, tort
law remedies were “clearly the ones presupposed by the
Framers of the Fourth Amendment and counterpart state
constitutional provisions.  . . . Indeed, the idea of exclusion
was so implausible that it seems almost never to have been
urged by criminal defendants, despite the large incentive
that they had to do so, in the vast number of criminal cases

26
litigated in the century after Independence.” Akhil Reed
Amar, The Constitution and Criminal Procedure: First
Principles 21 (1997). Mapp imposed an exclusionary-rule
regime on the states—even though most of the states did
not generally apply the exclusionary rule when Mapp was
decided. See Paul G. Cassell, The Mysterious Creation
of Search and Seizure Exclusionary Rules Under State
Constitutions: The Utah Example, 1993 Utah L. Rev. 751,
793–94 n.272. If Williams —which at least considered
the relevant history—is to be overruled because it is
insufficiently originalist, presumably Mapp must fall too.
Resting on even more dubious originalist foundations
is Miranda v. Arizona, 384 U.S. 436 (1966). See generally
Office of Legal Pol’y, U.S. Dept. of Justice, Report to the
Attorney General on the Law of Pre-trial Interrogation
(1986), reprinted in 22 Mich. J.L. Reform 437 (1989).
The 5–4 Miranda decision imposed a new warnings-andwaiver regime on all fifty states that none had followed
before. See, e.g., Miranda , 384 U.S. at 531 (White, J.,
dissenting) (“[T]he Court’s holding today is neither
compelled nor even strongly suggested by the language
of the Fifth Amendment, is at odds with American and
English legal history, and involves a departure from a
long line of precedent.”). Nonetheless, in Dickerson v.
United States, this Court chose to retain the ahistorical
Miranda  rules—even though Congress had passed a
statute replacing them—because the Court believed
that the warnings “have become part of our national
culture.” 530 U.S. 428, 443 (2000). Not only is Miranda
divorced from any historical connection, but it continues
to inflict untold harm on America’s criminal justice system
today. See generally Paul G. Cassell & Richard Fowles,
Still Handcuffing the Cops? A Review of Fifty Years of

27
Empirical Evidence of Miranda’s Harmful Effects on
Law Enforcement , 97 B.U. L. Rev. 685 (2017).
To maintain the consistent, evenhanded application of
stare decisis to cases implicating crime victims’ interests,
the Court should adhere to Williams rather than engage
in what might be called “one-way originalism”—adopting
a strict historical understanding of the Constitution when
it serves the interests of criminal defendants but turning
a blind eye to original public meaning when crime victims’
interests are implicated.
II. If this Court Overrules Williams , It Should
Also Hold that Traditional Protections Against
Overturning Otherwise Valid Criminal Convictions
Remain in Place.
For all the reasons just explained, this Court should
reach the same conclusion as Williams and allow Utah and
other states to continue using fewer-than-twelve-person
juries. If the Court nonetheless determines to overrule
Williams, it should make clear that any newly identified
“error” in jury size can be harmless. B.R.’s case illustrates
the importance of such clarification.
A constitutional error at trial generally does not
require automatic reversal. Chapman v. California , 386
U.S. 18, 21–22 (1967). Instead, an error usually requires
reversal only if it was likely to have affected the outcome.
Id. Thus, “most constitutional errors can be harmless.”
Neder v. United States , 527 U.S. 1, 8 (1999). If the
defendant had the assistance of counsel in a trial with an
impartial adjudicator, “there is a strong presumption”
that any errors are subject to harmless-error analysis. Id.

28
The harmless-error analysis in this case is quite
different from that in Ramos. When a jury verdict is not
unanimous, by definition at least one presumed-to-bereasonable juror concluded that the defendant had not
been proven guilty. An error in a criminal case can only be
“harmless if without the error no reasonable juror would
have voted to acquit.” United States v. Williams, 698 F .3d
374, 383 (7th Cir. 2012) (emphasis added). Thus, a fortiori,
where one reasonable juror has voted to acquit, the error
of not requiring unanimity is automatically harmful.
Indeed, in Ramos, perhaps because of this syllogism, no
one argued that a jury-unanimity error could be harmless.
590 U.S. at 111.
Here, by contrast, in many cases it can easily be shown
that no reasonable juror added to the case would have
reached a different result. B.R.’s case is one such example.
Eight presumably reasonable jurors unanimously found
that the defendant was guilty. And the evidence of guilt was
overwhelming, as outlined in the statement of facts above.
Trevino even admitted to some of the crimes. Adding
jurors #9, #10, #11, and #12—who must be presumed to
act reasonably—would have made no difference.
To be sure, this Court has held that certain “structural
errors” are not subject to harmless-error review. See
Weaver v. Massachusetts , 582 U.S. 286, 294 (2017).  But
the structural-error exception applies only to a “very
limited class of cases.” Neder, 527 U.S. at 8 (quoting
Johnson v. United States , 520 U.S. 461, 468 (1997))
(citing denial of counsel, a biased trial judge, racial
discrimination in grand-jury selection, denial of the
right to self-representation, denial of a public trial, and a
defective reasonable-doubt instruction as paradigmatic
examples). Indeed, “the defining feature of a structural

29
error is that it ‘affects the framework within which the
trial proceeds,’ rather than being ‘simply an error in the
trial process itself.’” Weaver, 582 U.S. at 295 (quoting
Arizona v. Fulminante, 499 U.S. 279, 310 (1991)) (citation
modified). Thus, an error is structural if: “the error always
results in fundamental unfairness”; “the right at issue
is not designed to protect the defendant from erroneous
conviction but instead protects some other interest”; or
“the effects of the error are simply too hard to measure.”
Id. at 295–96.
None of these three circumstances apply here. First,
nothing is “fundamentally unfair” about using fewer than
twelve jurors. Utah has been doing so for 130 years and,
so far as counsel can determine, there are only a couple
of reported appellate cases in which a criminal defendant
even questioned the approach. See State v. Barlow , 771
P .2d 662, 662 (Utah Ct. App. 1989) (“The Williams
decision left considerations of jury size to Congress and
the states ….” (internal quotation omitted); Johnson, 429
F .2d at 1154 (10th Cir. 1970) (same).
Like Utah, Florida has been using fewer-than-twelveperson juries since the late nineteenth century. And many
other states adopted fewer-than-twelve-person juries
only after this Court explicitly approved the practice in
Williams. It would be one thing to question the result in
Williams; but it would be quite another to suggest that
multiple states have treated tens of thousands of criminal
defendants with fundamental unfairness by using a
procedure this Court specifically approved.
Second, Petitioner himself argues that the commonlaw rule requiring twelve jurors was designed, at least
in part, to protect against erroneous convictions. Pet. Br.

30
at 3, 34–35. Although B.R. disputes that using fewer than
twelve jurors in fact results in appreciable numbers of
erroneous convictions, see supra Section I.C, such a rule
is significantly different in kind than the dignity interests
at stake in other rights that fall into this structural error
category, such as the right to conduct one’s own defense
without an attorney. See Weaver, 582 U.S. at 295.
Third, the effect of any error in jury size is not difficult
to determine. Lower courts can simply follow the standard
harmless-error approach of reviewing the evidence and
determining whether any reasonable juror could disagree
with the verdict the jury rendered. The claim that it would
be impossible to make such an assessment founders on
the fact that some lower courts have already made such
harmless-error determinations. See, e.g., United States v.
Johnson, 117 F .4th 28, 43–44 (2d Cir. 2024) (finding that
the case was “not close” and that  “[o]ne additional juror
participating in the deliberation would not have affected
the outcome on the counts that resulted in conviction”),
en banc denied , 143 F .4th 184 (2d Cir. 2025).
Automatically reversing all unanimous jury convictions
in felony cases currently on direct appeal from multiple
states14 would be a blunderbuss approach that would upset
thousands of convictions without regard to the weight
of the evidence. This Court has cautioned that “[t]he
14.  No plausible argument can be made for extending federal
habeas review to jury-size errors, even assuming Williams
were to be overruled. See Edwards v. Vannoy , 593 U.S. 255
(2021) (holding that Ramos did not apply retroactively on federal
collateral review); but cf. Watkins v. Ackley , 523 P.3d 86, 102–03
(Or. 2022) (extending state habeas relief to convictions obtained
by non-unanimous juries, following Ramos).

31
reversal of a conviction entails substantial social costs:
it forces jurors, witnesses, courts, the prosecution, and
the defendants to expend further time, energy, and other
resources to repeat a trial that has already once taken
place; victims may be asked to relive their disturbing
experiences.” United States v. Mechanik , 475 U.S. 66,
72 (1986). Indeed, in some cases, the “[p]assage of time,
erosion of memory, and dispersion of witnesses may render
retrial difficult, even impossible.” Id. (citation omitted).
Thus, while reversal “may, in theory, entitle the defendant
only to retrial, in practice it may reward the accused
with complete freedom from prosecution,” and thereby
“cost society the right to punish admitted offenders.” Id.
(citation omitted).
Even if a defendant is ultimately convicted in a second
trial, “the intervening delay may compromise society’s
interest in the prompt administration of justice, and
impede accomplishment of the objectives of deterrence
and rehabilitation.” Id. (citation omitted).  To be sure,
these “costs of reversal and retrial are an acceptable
and often necessary consequence when an error in
the first proceeding has deprived a defendant of a fair
determination of the issue of guilt or innocence. But the
balance of interest tips decidedly the other way when an
error has had no  effect on the outcome of the trial.” Id.

32
CONCLUSION
This Court should reaffirm Williams and affirm the
judgment below.
Respectfully submitted,

pages.text:
Appendix
2a
“Average population – 1990 & 2020” is the average of
the 1990 and 2020 state population figures, taken from
Historical Population Change Data (1910-2020) , U.S.
Census Bureau, https://www.census.gov/data/tables/
time-series/dec/popchange-data-text.html.  Note: All
population figures are millions rounded to one decimal
place. Arithmetic summations and averaging of the groups
of states performed using standard artificial intelligence
calculators.
The “7 states” are the seven states using fewer-thantwelve-person juries in felony cases, namely, Florida,
Arizona, Connecticut, Indiana, Louisiana, Massachusetts,
and Utah.  The “43 states” are the remainder.
The “6 states” are the same as the 7 states above,
excluding Louisiana (which used non-unanimous juries
for a significant part of the time frame above).  The “42
states” are the same as the 43 states above, excluding
Oregon (which used non-unanimous juries for a significant
part of the time frame above).
“Exonerations per capita” are the number of exonerations
for the state (or, collectively, group of states) divided by the
population for the state (or, collectively, group of states),
per 100,000 persons.
